item.title: Event Driven Architecture Doesn’t Eliminate Coupling
item.description: So you make what seems like a harmless change to an event that you’re publishing. Suddenly, a consumer of that event starts behaving incorrectly, and you’re left wondering, “I thought event driven architecture was supposed to prevent these issues. We replace direct API calls with events, put a message broker in the middle, and now… Read More » Event Driven Architecture Doesn’t Eliminate Coupling Worth a read for developers following Architecture.

item.title: Adding custom OpenTelemetry spans so an AI agent can see inside a request
item.description: The three Aspire posts of this series read telemetry that was already there. The first one counted the spans of a slow request, the second one needed the logs that went with them, the third one needed the metrics of the process. The answer was in the data every time. This time it is not. The slow endpoint runs one query, the query takes 2 ms, and the request takes 371 ms.

item.title: .NET MAUI 11 Makes CoreCLR the Default Runtime and Adds Incremental XAML Hot Reload

The release also adds device test templates and passkey support, and raises the minimum Android and Apple platform versions. By Edin Kapić Worth a read for developers following .NET. Link to article: https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/11/dotnet-maui-11-coreclr-hotreload

item.title: Diagnosing latency under load from Aspire metrics with an AI agent
item.description: In the first post about Aspire, the slow request had 203 spans. In the second one, it called another service once per line of a cart. In both cases, the trace of the slow request contained the explanation. This time it does not. The slow endpoint runs a single query, which takes less than a millisecond, and the request takes 170 ms. The trace shows a gap, and a gap has no attributes.

item.title: Debugging a running .NET application with WinDbg and an AI agent
item.description: Every post in this series so far started from a file: a dump, a gcdump, a trace. That works as long as the answer is in memory at the moment the file is written. Some answers never are. A dump can show that a value is wrong. It cannot show who wrote it, because by the time the dump is taken, the write is long gone. That question needs a debugger attached to the running process, one that stops the process…
